findings.summary: The worked SE(b2) example plugs the standard deviation of price (~37,000) in place of the regression standard error s_e and uses a wrong SD of size (360 instead of 398), producing 19.1 and then a spurious explanation ('smaller because the relationship is quite strong') for why the actual SE is 11.17.

- Sample size: n = 29
- Standard error of regression: σ_u ≈ 37,000
- Standard deviation of size: σ_x ≈ 360
- Estimated SE(b₂) = 37,000 / (√29 × 360) ≈ 19.1

(Actual SE is 11.17, smaller because the relationship is quite strong)
findings.new:
- Sample size: n = 29
- Standard error of regression: s_e ≈ 23,551
- Standard deviation of size: σ_x ≈ 398
- Estimated SE(b₂) = 23,551 / (√29 × 398) ≈ 11.0

(Actual SE is 11.17; the shortcut formula is slightly smaller because it uses √n in place of √(n-1))
findings.evidence: Exec dump CELL 2: SD(price)=37,390.7, SD(size)=398.27; CELL 3: RMSE=22,724.06 → s_e = 22,724.06×√(29/27) = 23,550.7 (matches pre-verified seed truth 23,550.66). The prose's 37,000 is the SD of y, not s_e. Correct inputs give 23,551/(√29×398) = 10.99 ≈ 11.0, matching the actual SE 11.17 (exact with √(n−1): 23,551/(√28×398.27) = 11.17), so the 'relationship is quite strong' rationale for the 19.1-vs-11.17 gap is spurious.
findings.verify_note: Real defect. Exec CELL 2 shows sd(price)=37,390.7 (that is sigma_y, mislabeled as sigma_u) and sd(size)=398.27 (not 360). CELL 3 RMSE=22,724.06 -> s_e = 22,724.06*sqrt(29/27) = 23,550.7 ~ 23,551. Correct inputs give 23,551/(sqrt(29)*398) = 10.99 ~ 11.0, essentially matching the true SE 11.17 (exact via sqrt(n-1): 23,551/(sqrt(28)*398.27)=11.18). The original 'smaller because the relationship is quite strong' rationale for the fake 19.1-vs-11.17 gap is spurious. Proposed fix (s_e~23,551, sigma_x~398, ~11.0, sqrt(n) vs sqrt(n-1) explanation) is correct.

findings.summary: The computed t-statistic formula writes the unknown population parameter σ_u in the denominator, contradicting the chapter's own emphasis that the computed t uses the estimate s_e (which is precisely why T(n−2) replaces N(0,1)).
findings.old: $$t = \frac{b_2}{se(b_2)} = \frac{b_2}{\sigma_u / \sqrt{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2}}$$
findings.new: $$t = \frac{b_2}{se(b_2)} = \frac{b_2}{s_e / \sqrt{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2}}$$
findings.evidence: The chapter states at L532 'The problem: We never know σ_u in practice!' and defines the feasible statistic with s_e at L534–538; the sample statistic t = b2/se(b2) is computed from s_e, so σ_u in this denominator conflates the Z and T constructions the section works hard to distinguish.
findings.verify_note: The claim that L850 must use s_e misreads the chapter's dual notation. The chapter's SE formula uses sigma_u at L314 (se(b2)=sigma_u/(sqrt(n)*sigma_x)) and again at L1166 (se(b2)=sigma_u/sqrt(sum(x-xbar)^2)); the s_e substitution appears only in the Z-vs-T sampling-distribution subsection (L530/L536). L850 reproduces the chapter's own theoretical se(b2) formula, so it is internally consistent with L314/L1166. Changing sigma_u->s_e at L850 ALONE would desync it from those two other identical formulas. There is a genuine technical looseness (calling it 't' while using population sigma_u), but the single-site fix as proposed is not decisively correct; a proper fix would harmonize L314, L1166, and L850 together (or leave all three as the theoretical formula).
